rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: Find the vector equation of a line passing through a point with position vector \(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and parallel to the line joining the points \(-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and \(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\).
rows.solution: A line is fixed by a point on it and a vector parallel to it, so the only work is finding the direction. Two lines are parallel when they share a direction vector, and the direction of the line joining the two given points is the difference of their position vectors: \(\left(\hat{i} + 2\hat{j} + 2\hat{k}\right) - \left(-\hat{i} + 4\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\). The required line passes through the point with position vector \(\vec{a} = 2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\) and is parallel to \(\vec{b} = 2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\). Using \(\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda\vec{b}\), the vector equation of the line is \(\vec{r} = \left(2\hat{i} - \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) + \lambda\left(2\hat{i} - 2\hat{j} + \hat{k}\right)\), where \(\lambda\) is a scalar parameter.

rows.stem: Let \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} + \hat{j}\), \(\vec{b} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}\) and \(\vec{c} = \hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\). If \(\hat{n}\) is a unit vector such that \(\vec{a} \cdot \hat{n} = 0\) and \(\vec{b} \cdot \hat{n} = 0\), then find \(\left|\vec{c} \cdot \hat{n}\right|\).
rows.solution: A zero dot product means perpendicularity, so \(\vec{a} \cdot \hat{n} = 0\) and \(\vec{b} \cdot \hat{n} = 0\) say that \(\hat{n}\) is perpendicular to both \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\). The vector perpendicular to two given vectors is their cross product, so \(\hat{n} = \pm\dfrac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}\). Here \(\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \end{vmatrix} = \hat{i}(0 - 0) - \hat{j}(0 - 0) + \hat{k}(-1 - 1) = -2\hat{k}\), whose magnitude is \(2\). Hence \(\hat{n} = -\hat{k}\) (or equally \(\hat{n} = \hat{k}\), since the question only fixes \(\hat{n}\) up to sign). Therefore \(\left|\vec{c} \cdot \hat{n}\right| = \left|\left(\hat{i} + \hat{j} + \hat{k}\right) \cdot \left(-\hat{k}\right)\right| = |-1| = 1\). The modulus is what makes the sign ambiguity harmless, and the required value is \(1\).

rows.stem: If \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are unit vectors inclined at an angle \(30^\circ\) to each other, then find the area of the parallelogram with \(\left(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}\right)\) and \(\left(3\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right)\) as adjacent sides.
rows.solution: The area of a parallelogram with adjacent sides \(\vec{p}\) and \(\vec{q}\) is \(|\vec{p} \times \vec{q}|\), so expand the cross product using its distributive property: \(\left(\vec{a} + 3\vec{b}\right) \times \left(3\vec{a} + \vec{b}\right) = 3\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{a}\right) + \left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right) + 9\left(\vec{b} \times \vec{a}\right) + 3\left(\vec{b} \times \vec{b}\right)\). The cross product of a vector with itself is the zero vector, so the first and last terms vanish, and \(\vec{b} \times \vec{a} = -\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right)\) by anti-commutativity. This leaves \(\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right) - 9\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right) = -8\left(\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right)\). Taking magnitudes, the area is \(8\left|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}\right| = 8|\vec{a}||\vec{b}|\sin 30^{\circ}\). Since \(\vec{a}\) and \(\vec{b}\) are unit vectors, \(|\vec{a}| = |\vec{b}| = 1\), so the area is \(8 \times 1 \times 1 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 4\) square units.

No antiderivative of this integrand is available, so use the property \(\int_0^a f(x)\,dx = \int_0^a f(a - x)\,dx\) with \(a = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). First write the integrand in terms of sine and cosine: since \(\tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}\), \(I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{dx}{1 + \dfrac{\sin^{2/3} x}{\cos^{2/3} x}} = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^{2/3} x}{\cos^{2/3} x + \sin^{2/3} x}\,dx\) ... (I). Now replace \(x\) by \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\), which interchanges sine and cosine: \(I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\sin^{2/3} x}{\sin^{2/3} x + \cos^{2/3} x}\,dx\) ... (II). The two integrands share a denominator and their numerators add to it exactly, so adding (I) and (II) gives \(2I = \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{\cos^{2/3} x + \sin^{2/3} x}{\cos^{2/3} x + \sin^{2/3} x}\,dx = \int_0^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\). Hence \(I = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\).

rows.stem: In a factory, machine A produces 30% of total output, machine B produces 25% and the machine C produces the remaining output. The defective items produced by machines A, B and C are 1%, 1.2%, 2% respectively. An item is picked at random from a day's output and found to be defective. Find the probability that it was produced by machine B?
rows.solution: The defect is observed and the machine is to be inferred, so this is Bayes' theorem. Let \(E_1\), \(E_2\), \(E_3\) be the events that the item was produced by machine A, B, C respectively, and \(F\) the event that the item is defective. Machine C makes the remaining \(100 - 30 - 25 = 45\) per cent, so \(P(E_1) = \dfrac{30}{100}\), \(P(E_2) = \dfrac{25}{100}\), \(P(E_3) = \dfrac{45}{100}\), while the defect rates give \(P(F \mid E_1) = \dfrac{1}{100}\), \(P(F \mid E_2) = \dfrac{1.2}{100}\), \(P(F \mid E_3) = \dfrac{2}{100}\). By Bayes' theorem, \(P(E_2 \mid F) = \dfrac{P(E_2)P(F \mid E_2)}{P(E_1)P(F \mid E_1) + P(E_2)P(F \mid E_2) + P(E_3)P(F \mid E_3)}\). Every term carries a factor \(\dfrac{1}{100} \times \dfrac{1}{100}\), which cancels, so the ratio reduces to \(\dfrac{25 \times 1.2}{30 \times 1 + 25 \times 1.2 + 45 \times 2} = \dfrac{30}{30 + 30 + 90} = \dfrac{30}{150} = \dfrac{1}{5}\). Hence the probability that the defective item came from machine B is \(\dfrac{1}{5}\).
